60	\label{sec:diagnostic}
61	
62	The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
63	This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:
64	
65	\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
66	\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
67	\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
68	\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
69	  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
70	  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
71	  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
72	  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. When concentration falls below 0.50, the top-5\% heads contribute too little cumulative delta for the solver to construct a meaningfully non-uniform allocation; consequently the $t_1/t_5$ ratio---regardless of its value---does not alter the outcome, and concentration alone suffices to determine the category. Mistral (0.24, $t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.38$): counterproductive.
73	  \end{itemize}
74	\end{enumerate}
75	
76	Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
77	Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
78	The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
79	Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
80	The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
81	Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Heterogeneity Characterization}
\label{sec:heterogeneity}

The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on how unevenly head sensitivities are distributed.
We quantify this with a \emph{top-5\% concentration metric}: sort per-head 2-bit distortions $d_h(2)$ in descending order and compute the fraction of total distortion contributed by the top 5\% of heads.
High concentration indicates that a few heads are disproportionately sensitive; low concentration indicates near-uniform sensitivity.

Table~\ref{tab:heterogeneity} summarizes the results across five architectures at $4\times$ compression.
The central finding is that MCKP benefit requires \emph{spread heterogeneity}---multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients---rather than sensitivity concentrated in a single outlier at one bitwidth.

Qwen2.5-7B exemplifies the spread pattern (top-5\% concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$), with Layer-0 heads contributing the majority of total 2-bit distortion across multiple bitwidths.
Constrained MCKP reduces degradation from $+$5.64 PPL (uniform) to $+$1.42 PPL, a 27.3\% improvement over uniform 4-bit. %exp_id=qwen_constrained_mckp

Yi-1.5-9B is a critical counterexample: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen's $0.61$), constrained MCKP matches uniform ($+$0.20 vs.\ $+$0.20). %exp_id=yi15_hires_constrained_mckp
The mechanism is clear from the cross-bitwidth gradient structure.
Yi-1.5's sensitivity is dominated by a single extreme outlier: Layer-4 Head-3 has a 2-bit delta of 13.12, while the second-ranked head has delta 0.55---a $24\times$ gap ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$, $t_1/t_2{=}23.7$). %exp_id=yi15_hires_profiling
Critically, L4H3's sensitivity is confined to the 2-bit operating point: its 4-bit and 8-bit deltas are ${\approx}\,0$.
The solver therefore has only one lever---upgrading L4H3 from 2-bit to 4-bit removes the distortion, but further upgrading to 8-bit provides no additional benefit, so the budget freed by downgrading other heads has nowhere useful to go.
This is the ``spike'' pattern: high concentration driven by a single outlier with sensitivity at only one bitwidth.

In contrast, Qwen's Layer-0 heads exhibit non-zero deltas at multiple bitwidths (e.g., L0H0: 2-bit delta ${=}6.74$, with positive 4-bit and 8-bit deltas), giving the solver a multi-bitwidth sensitivity gradient across several heads---a ``spread'' pattern that enables meaningful budget reallocation. %exp_id=qwen_hires_profiling

The remaining three architectures fill out the diagnostic picture.
Llama-3.1-8B shows above-threshold concentration ($0.57$) with a pronounced spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, $t_1/t_2{=}34.8$); its allocation is essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($+$0.36 vs.\ $+$0.38). %exp_id=llama_hires_bf16_2bitonly %exp_id=llama_hires_constrained
Mistral-7B-v0.3 ($t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2-9B ($t_1/t_5{=}0.38$) both exhibit flat distributions with low concentration ($0.24$ and $0.23$ respectively), leaving the profiler with no reliable signal; constrained MCKP is slightly worse than uniform in both cases ($+$0.13 vs.\ $+$0.10 for Mistral; $+$0.15 vs.\ $+$0.13 for Gemma-2). %exp_id=mistral_c4_cross_dataset %exp_id=gemma2_full_pipeline

\subsection{Diagnostic Framework}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

The heterogeneity characterization shows that MCKP benefit requires not just high concentration but a specific \emph{shape}---spread heterogeneity across multiple heads with cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients.
This motivates a joint diagnostic, based on five architectures, for deciding when non-uniform allocation is worthwhile:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item Run per-head profiling as described in \S\ref{sec:profiling}.
\item Compute the top-5\% concentration and the $t_1/t_5$ ratio (top-1 distortion divided by top-5 distortion) from the resulting distortion table.
\item Select allocation strategy based on concentration \emph{and} shape:
  \begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Spread} (concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$, $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$): non-uniform allocation recommended. Multiple heads exhibit cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradients, giving the solver room to redistribute budget. Qwen (0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$): 27.3\% PPL improvement.
  \item \textbf{Spike} ($t_1/t_5 \gtrsim 0.70$, any concentration): use uniform. Sensitivity is dominated by a single outlier with no cross-bitwidth gradient; the solver cannot exploit it. Yi-1.5 (0.71, $t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) and Llama (0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$): no meaningful benefit.
  \item \textbf{Flat} (concentration $\lesssim 0.50$): use uniform. Near-uniform sensitivity provides no signal for differentiated allocation. When concentration falls below 0.50, the top-5\% heads contribute too little cumulative delta for the solver to construct a meaningfully non-uniform allocation; consequently the $t_1/t_5$ ratio---regardless of its value---does not alter the outcome, and concentration alone suffices to determine the category. Mistral (0.24, $t_1/t_5{=}0.41$) and Gemma-2 (0.23, $t_1/t_5{=}0.38$): counterproductive.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

Llama-3.1-8B illustrates why both conditions are needed: its concentration (0.57) lies above the 0.50 threshold and would be misclassified as beneficial by concentration alone, but its spike shape ($t_1/t_5{=}0.85$) correctly predicts no meaningful benefit.
Indeed, a concentration-only threshold would misclassify two of the three high-concentration models (Yi-1.5 at 0.71 and Llama at 0.57), making the $t_1/t_5$ shape condition essential for avoiding false positives.
The joint condition---concentration $\gtrsim 0.50$ and $t_1/t_5 \lesssim 0.70$---correctly separates the beneficial case from the four non-beneficial cases across all five architectures studied.
Both thresholds are illustrative, derived from five models; they should be validated on a broader set before being treated as general rules.
The diagnostic adds no computational overhead: it reuses the profiling data already required for the allocation solver and avoids wasted optimization effort on architectures where non-uniform allocation provides no benefit.
Additional analyses---the effect of aggressive compression ratios, profiling resolution and multi-seed stability, per-layer optimality validation, and KV separation ablation---are provided in Appendices~\ref{sec:aggressive}--\ref{sec:kv_separation}.

\small
\caption{Constrained MCKP vs.\ heuristic baselines at 4$\times$ compression. L0-random reports median and mean$\pm$std over 5 seeds. All methods use per-model optimal $k$ ($k{=}8$ for Qwen, $k{=}2$ for Llama, $k{=}4$ for Mistral). Llama and Mistral use hires profiling, consistent with Table~\ref{tab:main_results}.}
\label{tab:heuristic}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Model & MCKP & \multicolumn{2}{c}{L0-random} & Naive \\
 & & Median & Mean$\pm$Std & Positional \\
\midrule
Qwen2.5-7B      & 11.23 & 11.52 & 11.69$\pm$0.47 & 12.23 \\
Llama-3.1-8B    & 8.45  & 8.62  & 8.62$\pm$0.07  & 8.58 \\
Mistral-7B-v0.3 & 7.16  & 7.20  & 7.24$\pm$0.07  & 7.21 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:heuristic} compares profiling-guided MCKP against heuristic baselines that use the same Layer-0 protection but assign 2-bit heads without profiling.

On Qwen, MCKP (11.23) beats the L0-random median (11.52) by 0.29 PPL and the naive positional heuristic (12.23) by 1.00 PPL, confirming that profiling-guided selection outperforms both random and depth-based assignment.

On Llama ($k{=}2$), the gap between methods is small: MCKP achieves 8.45 vs.\ L0-random 8.62 and naive positional 8.58.
With only 2 heads assigned to 2-bit, the choice of which heads to compress has limited impact, and all methods cluster within 0.17 PPL.
MCKP still achieves the best result, but the practical advantage of profiling-guided selection is negligible at this constraint level.

On Mistral ($k{=}4$), all non-uniform strategies are worse than uniform 4-bit (7.13): MCKP 7.16, naive 7.21, L0-random median 7.20 (mean 7.24$\pm$0.07).
MCKP outperforms both heuristics, but the best non-uniform result (7.16) still exceeds uniform by 0.03 PPL, reinforcing that non-uniform allocation is counterproductive when heterogeneity is low.
Note that the heuristic baselines use a slightly higher budget (0.256 vs.\ 0.248 for MCKP, a 3\% difference) because integer $k$ does not divide evenly into the target; despite this advantage, they still underperform MCKP, making the comparison conservative.

\subsection{Downstream Evaluation}
\label{sec:downstream}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{0-shot accuracy on Qwen2.5-7B at 4$\times$ compression. Constrained MCKP recovers approximately 73\% of the accuracy lost by uniform 4-bit quantization.}
\label{tab:downstream}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Task & Baseline & Uniform & MCKP & $\Delta$ vs \\
 & (bf16) & (4-bit) & (Ours) & Uniform \\
\midrule
ARC-C      & ---   & 0.482 & 0.514 & $+$3.2 pts \\
HellaSwag  & ---   & 0.728 & 0.768 & $+$4.0 pts \\
PIQA       & ---   & 0.766 & 0.779 & $+$1.3 pts \\
WinoGrande & ---   & 0.662 & 0.682 & $+$2.0 pts \\
\midrule
Average    & 0.695 & 0.660 & 0.686 & $+$2.6 pts \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:downstream} shows that the PPL improvements transfer to downstream tasks on Qwen2.5-7B.
Constrained MCKP improves average 0-shot accuracy by 2.6 points over uniform 4-bit (0.686 vs.\ 0.660), with gains on all four benchmarks.
The largest gain appears on HellaSwag ($+$4.0 pts), where language modeling quality is most directly reflected.

Constrained MCKP recovers approximately 73\% of the accuracy lost by uniform 4-bit quantization, indicating that per-head bit allocation addresses much of the degradation, though a gap to bf16 remains.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Stability}
\label{sec:cross_dataset}

To verify that the profiled allocation is not overfit to the calibration corpus, we profile on C4 and evaluate on WikiText-2, and vice versa, at $4\times$ compression.
On Qwen2.5-7B, C4-calibrated MCKP achieves 11.29 PPL on WikiText-2 (vs.\ 15.45 uniform, a 27\% reduction), only 0.06 PPL above the WikiText-2-calibrated result (11.23).
In the reverse direction, WikiText-2-calibrated MCKP achieves 20.56 PPL on the C4 held-out split (vs.\ 35.42 uniform, a 42\% reduction; C4 bf16 baseline on this split is 15.32).
All three models show ${>}96\%$ bit-assignment agreement across calibration sources: Qwen 96.4\% (108/112 heads), Llama 97.7\% (250/256), and Mistral 96.5\% (247/256).
Qwen's agreement is the most informative, as all 112 heads have variable assignments; on Llama, 253 of 256 heads are forced to 4-bit by the $k{=}2$ constraint, inflating agreement.
The cross-dataset results reinforce the heterogeneity-driven narrative: on Qwen, the MCKP benefit is preserved across calibration sources; on Llama and Mistral, the lack of benefit is equally stable---Llama's C4-calibrated MCKP is 0.18 PPL worse than uniform, and Mistral shows similar degradation ($-$0.03 to $-$0.05 PPL).
Whether non-uniform allocation helps is determined by the model's intrinsic head sensitivity heterogeneity, not the calibration data.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Per-head mixed-precision quantization of the KV cache is a natural strategy for reducing memory during LLM inference: assign fewer bits to insensitive heads and more bits to sensitive ones, achieving lower perplexity than uniform quantization at the same average bit-width.
Recent work on KV cache quantization explores both uniform schemes~\cite{liu2024kivi,hooper2024kvquant,lin2024qserve,he2024zipcache} and token-level mixed-precision approaches~\cite{ge2024fastgen,lei2026arkv}, while complementary methods reduce cache size through eviction~\cite{zhang2023h2o,li2024snapkv}.
RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} formalizes per-head allocation as a rate-distortion optimization and shows that greedy allocation is optimal when bit-widths are consecutive integers $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, exploiting the polymatroid structure of the feasible set (their Proposition~6).

In practice, hardware-efficient inference requires bit-widths drawn from $\{2, 4, 8, 16\}$---the formats natively supported by modern accelerators.
On this non-consecutive set, the polymatroid structure breaks down, and greedy is no longer provably optimal.
One might expect that exact MCKP solvers would fill this gap.
They do not.
On Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression, unconstrained greedy achieves 32.45 PPL and unconstrained MCKP achieves 36.92---both \emph{far worse} than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
The optimization does not merely underperform; it fails catastrophically.

The root cause is not solver suboptimality but a violation of the objective's additive distortion assumption.
Both solvers assign 68--75 of 112 KV heads to 2-bit, where per-head quantization errors are large enough to compound through the residual stream.
The additive model predicts $\sim$11 PPL for these allocations; the actual PPL is $3$--$4\times$ higher.
At 4-bit and above, per-head distortions are small and compound negligibly---uniform 4-bit achieves close to its additive prediction---but 2-bit distortions are orders of magnitude larger.
When most heads are quantized to 2-bit simultaneously, cumulative truncation errors exceed the network's capacity to compensate, and perplexity degrades super-linearly.

This observation points to a minimal intervention: cap the number of 2-bit assignments.
We add a single cardinality constraint $\sum_h \mathbb{1}[b_h{=}2] \leq k$ to the standard MCKP formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}).
On Qwen2.5-7B, setting $k{=}8$ (7\% of heads) yields 11.23 PPL---a 27.3\% reduction over uniform 4-bit.
The constraint works by forcing the solver to use 2-bit only on the least-sensitive heads, while redistributing the freed budget to protect sensitive heads at 8-bit or 16-bit.
This is not a heuristic patch: the constraint directly addresses the identified failure mode and is compatible with any solver.

A surprising consequence is that, under the cardinality constraint, the choice of solver becomes irrelevant.
Constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce identical allocations---not approximately, but exactly: all 112 heads receive the same bit-width on Qwen2.5-7B, all 256 on Llama-3.1-8B, and 255 of 256 on Mistral-7B-v0.3 (the single difference is a zero-distortion tie with no PPL impact).
The constraint narrows the feasible set enough that greedy's locally optimal decisions are globally optimal (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}), enabling practitioners to use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm without sacrificing solution quality.
A per-layer brute-force oracle confirms near-optimality: the maximum gap across 28 layers is 0.02 PPL, 0.4\% of the total improvement (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

However, non-uniform allocation does not help universally.
On Llama-3.1-8B, constrained MCKP achieves 8.45 PPL vs.\ uniform 8.47---essentially indistinguishable from uniform ($\Delta < 0.02$ PPL).
On Mistral-7B-v0.3, it is slightly \emph{worse}: 7.16 vs.\ 7.13.
On Yi-1.5-9B, non-uniform allocation provides no benefit (7.22 vs.\ 7.22 uniform) despite Yi-1.5 having the highest GQA ratio tested (8:1).
On Gemma-2-9B (GQA 2:1, the lowest ratio tested), degradation is 0.3\% (9.05 vs.\ 9.03).
The difference across architectures traces to head sensitivity heterogeneity---specifically, its \emph{distribution shape}, not GQA ratio alone.
Qwen's KV heads vary widely in 2-bit distortion, with Layer-0 heads forming a cluster of high sensitivity; Yi-1.5 has a single extreme outlier but otherwise uniform heads (a ``spike'' pattern that MCKP cannot exploit); Gemma-2 and Mistral show near-uniform sensitivity across all heads.
When there is no exploitable heterogeneity, non-uniform allocation adds noise without benefit.

This motivates a diagnostic question that prior work does not address: \emph{when} should a practitioner use per-head mixed-precision quantization?
We propose a joint heterogeneity diagnostic based on concentration \emph{and} distribution shape of per-head distortion (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
On our five architectures, the diagnostic separates the beneficial case (Qwen, concentration 0.61, spread pattern) from cases where non-uniform allocation provides no meaningful benefit.
Yi-1.5 is a critical test: its concentration ($0.71$) exceeds Qwen's, but its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike with no cross-bitwidth gradient---precisely the pattern where MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
The diagnostic reuses profiling data already required by the solver and adds no computational overhead.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item We identify 2-bit distortion compounding as the cause of catastrophic failure in unconstrained per-head KV cache quantization on hardware-aligned bit-widths, and show that a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments is a minimal sufficient fix, reducing Qwen2.5-7B PPL from 32--37 (unconstrained) to 11.23 (constrained) at $4\times$ compression (\S\ref{sec:compounding}, \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\item We demonstrate that the cardinality constraint makes solver choice irrelevant: constrained greedy and constrained MCKP produce equivalent per-head allocations across three architectures, enabling use of a simple greedy algorithm (\S\ref{sec:solver_equiv}).

\item We propose a joint diagnostic combining concentration and distribution shape ($t_1/t_5$ ratio) that correctly separates architectures where non-uniform allocation helps from those where it does not, across all five models tested. Yi-1.5-9B serves as a critical test: its concentration exceeds Qwen's, yet its single-outlier spike pattern means MCKP provides no benefit over uniform (\S\ref{sec:heterogeneity}).
\end{enumerate}

12	\label{sec:profiling_resolution}
13	
14	We compare standard-resolution profiling (16 sequences $\times$ 512 tokens) against high-resolution profiling (64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens) on Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression.
15	
16	High-resolution profiling improves constrained MCKP from 11.23 to 10.91 PPL ($-$0.32 absolute).
17	Relative to the bf16 baseline (9.81), this reduces the degradation from 1.42 to 1.10, a 22.5\% reduction.
18	The improvement comes from finer-grained sensitivity estimates: standard profiling detects non-zero 2-bit distortion in 37 of 112 heads, while high-resolution profiling detects 100 of 112 (2.7$\times$ more).
19	
20	The additional signal changes 8 of 112 head assignments.
21	High-resolution profiling protects shallow layers (L1--L3) at higher bit-widths while compressing mid-layers (L5--L11) more aggressively---a redistribution that standard profiling misses because its distortion estimates for these heads fall below the noise floor.
22	
23	\paragraph{Multi-seed stability.}
24	The profiled allocation is stable across calibration subsets.
25	Under hires profiling on Qwen2.5-7B, constrained MCKP yields mean PPL $10.99 \pm 0.06$ across 3 random calibration seeds (individual runs: 11.02, 10.90, 11.05), with std/mean below 0.6\%.
26	The bit distribution is identical across all seeds ($\{$2-bit: 8, 4-bit: 100, 8-bit: 4$\}$), and 101 of 112 heads (90.2\%) receive the same assignment in all three runs.
27	This stability confirms that the per-head sensitivity ranking is robust to calibration sampling noise.
28	
29	\paragraph{Numerical precision.}
30	Float32 profiling (64 $\times$ 2048 tokens) yields an identical constrained allocation and PPL within seed variance (10.89 vs.\ 10.91, $\Delta = 0.02 < \sigma = 0.06$), confirming that bfloat16 precision is sufficient for the profiling step.
31

33	To validate the additive distortion assumption underlying the MCKP formulation, we compare constrained MCKP against a per-layer brute-force oracle that exhaustively enumerates all $4^4 = 256$ bit-width combinations within each 4-head group on Qwen2.5-7B (hires profiling).
34	Of the 8 layers admitting multiple feasible allocations, MCKP matches the oracle exactly in 5; the remaining 3 show gaps of 0.018 (Layer~1), 0.014 (Layer~11), and 0.005 (Layer~4) PPL.
35	All three gaps involve repositioning a 2-bit assignment among heads with near-identical sensitivity within the same layer bit budget.

39	\label{sec:kv_separation}

This systematic asymmetry suggests that K caches are inherently more compressible than V caches, consistent with the observation that key vectors primarily encode positional information while value vectors carry content.

Joint allocation is sufficient under the current constraint formulation.
Separated K/V allocation with per-side cardinality constraints---limiting 2-bit assignments independently for K and V---is a direction for future work.

\section{Runtime Benchmark}
\label{sec:runtime}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{PyTorch-level latency on Qwen2.5-7B (single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96\,GB), prompt\_len=256, gen\_len=128, mean of 10 runs). All conditions store KV in bf16 with simulated per-head quantize/dequantize calls; peak GPU memory is identical across rows.}
\label{tab:runtime}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Condition & Prefill (ms) & Decode (ms/tok) & Throughput (tok/s) \\
\midrule
Baseline bf16       & 45.86 & 33.78 & 29.6 \\
Uniform 4-bit       & 54.25 & 42.46 & 23.6 \\
Constrained MCKP    & 57.03 & 46.09 & 21.8 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:runtime} reports end-to-end latency for three KV cache configurations.
Uniform 4-bit quantization adds 25.7\% decode overhead relative to the bf16 baseline (42.46 vs.\ 33.78~ms/tok), reflecting per-head quantize/dequantize calls at every attention step.
Constrained MCKP adds a further 8.5\% over uniform (46.09 vs.\ 42.46~ms/tok), because mixed-precision allocation dispatches different dequantization kernels for 2-bit, 4-bit, and 8-bit heads within the same layer.
The MCKP solver itself runs in ${\sim}5$~ms and is invoked once at initialization, contributing negligibly to end-to-end latency.
Both quantized conditions achieve the same $4\times$ KV cache compression (5.25~MB vs.\ 21~MB at bf16), so the latency difference between uniform and MCKP reflects only the mixed-precision dispatch overhead, not a memory trade-off.

\paragraph{Caveat.}
These measurements use PyTorch-level per-head \texttt{quantize}/\texttt{dequantize} calls and do \emph{not} represent optimized CUDA kernel performance.
Production inference engines such as vLLM and TensorRT-LLM employ fused attention kernels that batch dequantization with the matrix multiply, amortizing the per-head dispatch cost that dominates the gap between uniform and MCKP in our simulation.
The 8.5\% overhead reported here should therefore be treated as an upper bound on the mixed-precision penalty; real-world deployment with fused kernels would likely narrow or eliminate this gap.
The limitation noted in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}---that we report no real-kernel latency benchmarks---remains: the numbers above quantify simulation overhead, not production inference speedup.

1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	We showed that per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding through the residual stream.
4	A single constraint---limiting simultaneously active 2-bit heads to $k \leq 8$ (7\% of heads)---reduces perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement at $4\times$ compression.
5	Under the constraint, solver choice becomes irrelevant: greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all three architectures ($\Delta = 0.0000$), so a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm suffices.
6	The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on both the concentration and \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity.
7	Qwen2.5-7B (concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$, spread pattern) shows large gains; Llama-3.1-8B (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, spike) is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47 PPL); Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B show no benefit.
8	Yi-1.5-9B is a critical test case: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen), its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
9	A joint diagnostic using concentration ($\gtrsim 0.50$) and $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($\lesssim 0.70$) correctly identifies spread, spike, and flat patterns across all five models studied, computable from the same profiling pass used for allocation.
10	This provides a practical guideline: practitioners can determine whether non-uniform quantization is worthwhile for their architecture \emph{before} running the allocation solver.
11	
12	\paragraph{Limitations.}
13	Our study has several limitations that temper the generality of the findings.
14	First, we evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
15	Second, profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); alternative measures such as gradient-based or activation-norm diagnostics remain unexplored and could yield different allocation decisions.
16	Third, we report perplexity and downstream accuracy but no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
17	Fourth, we have not verified whether these findings transfer to larger scales (70B+), where head counts and attention patterns differ substantially.
18	Finally, although we validate on four downstream tasks, profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).
19	
20	\paragraph{Future Work.}
21	Extending evaluation to 70B+ models would test whether the heterogeneity--benefit relationship holds at scale.
22	Integration with production inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) would enable real-kernel latency measurement, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) or dynamic per-request allocation could further improve the framework.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We showed that per-head mixed-precision KV cache quantization over hardware-aligned bit-widths \{2, 4, 8, 16\} requires a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments to prevent non-additive distortion compounding through the residual stream.
A single constraint---limiting simultaneously active 2-bit heads to $k \leq 8$ (7\% of heads)---reduces perplexity on Qwen2.5-7B from 15.45 (uniform 4-bit) to 11.23, a 27.3\% improvement at $4\times$ compression.
Under the constraint, solver choice becomes irrelevant: greedy and MCKP produce equivalent allocations across all three architectures ($\Delta = 0.0000$), so a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm suffices.
The benefit of non-uniform allocation depends on both the concentration and \emph{shape} of head sensitivity heterogeneity.
Qwen2.5-7B (concentration 0.61, $t_1/t_5{=}0.57$, spread pattern) shows large gains; Llama-3.1-8B (concentration 0.57, $t_1/t_5{=}0.85$, spike) is essentially indistinguishable from uniform (8.45 vs.\ 8.47 PPL); Mistral-7B-v0.3, Yi-1.5-9B, and Gemma-2-9B show no benefit.
Yi-1.5-9B is a critical test case: despite the highest concentration tested ($0.71$, exceeding Qwen), its heterogeneity is a single-outlier spike ($t_1/t_5{=}0.90$) with no cross-bitwidth sensitivity gradient, so MCKP cannot redistribute budget.
A joint diagnostic using concentration ($\gtrsim 0.50$) and $t_1/t_5$ ratio ($\lesssim 0.70$) correctly identifies spread, spike, and flat patterns across all five models studied, computable from the same profiling pass used for allocation.
This provides a practical guideline: practitioners can determine whether non-uniform quantization is worthwhile for their architecture \emph{before} running the allocation solver.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Our study has several limitations that temper the generality of the findings.
First, we evaluate only five 7--9B-scale models---too few to establish a statistically robust correlation between heterogeneity and quantization benefit; the observed trend is directional evidence, not a predictive law.
Second, profiling relies on a single sensitivity metric (perplexity-based per-head distortion); alternative measures such as gradient-based or activation-norm diagnostics remain unexplored and could yield different allocation decisions.
Third, we report perplexity and downstream accuracy but no real-kernel latency benchmarks, leaving the practical inference speedup from mixed-precision allocation unquantified.
Fourth, we have not verified whether these findings transfer to larger scales (70B+), where head counts and attention patterns differ substantially.
Finally, although we validate on four downstream tasks, profiling and primary evaluation use a single dataset (WikiText-2).

\paragraph{Future Work.}
Extending evaluation to 70B+ models would test whether the heterogeneity--benefit relationship holds at scale.
Integration with production inference engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) would enable real-kernel latency measurement, and investigating per-side K/V cardinality constraints (Appendix~\ref{sec:kv_separation}) or dynamic per-request allocation could further improve the framework.

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
5	\label{sec:formulation}
6	
7	We formulate per-head KV cache quantization as a constrained optimization problem.
8	Let $h \in \{1,\ldots,H\}$ index the KV heads across all layers, $b_h \in \mathcal{B}$ the bit-width assigned to head $h$, and $\mathcal{B} = \{2, 4, 8, 16\}$ the set of hardware-aligned bit-widths.
9	Each head $h$ has a profiled distortion function $d_h(b)$, the PPL increase when head $h$ is quantized to $b$ bits.
10	Given a memory budget ratio $R$ (e.g., $R = 0.25$ for $4\times$ compression), we seek the allocation that minimizes total distortion:
11	\begin{equation}
12	\label{eq:objective}
13	\min_{\{b_h\}} \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_h(b_h) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \frac{1}{H \cdot 16}\sum_{h=1}^{H} b_h \leq R.
14	\end{equation}
15	
16	This is a multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP): each head selects one bit-width from $\mathcal{B}$ to minimize total distortion under a budget.
17	RateQuant~\cite{zuo2026ratequant} solves this for consecutive bit-widths $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, where the polymatroid structure of the feasible set guarantees that greedy allocation is optimal (their Proposition 6).
18	Hardware-aligned bit-widths $\{2,4,8,16\}$ are non-consecutive; the gaps break this structure, and greedy is no longer guaranteed to match the MCKP optimum.
19	Moreover, as we show in \S\ref{sec:compounding}, the objective itself is not well-behaved: distortions from 2-bit heads compound non-additively, making unconstrained optimization unreliable.
20	
21	\subsection{PPL-based Per-Head Profiling}
22	\label{sec:profiling}
23	
24	We profile each KV head independently by quantizing it to each $b \in \mathcal{B}$ while keeping all other heads at bf16, and measuring the resulting PPL increase $d_h(b)$ on a calibration set of 64 sequences $\times$ 2048 tokens from WikiText-2 train.
25	This yields a distortion table of $H \times |\mathcal{B}|$ entries that serves as input to the solver.
26	
27	The optimization in Eq.~\eqref{eq:objective} relies on an additive distortion assumption: the total PPL degradation from a mixed-precision allocation is approximately $\sum_h d_h(b_h)$.
28	This holds when per-head distortions are small and independent---a reasonable approximation for 4-bit and 8-bit quantization, where individual head distortions are typically below 0.1 PPL.
29	At 2-bit, however, individual distortions are orders of magnitude larger, and the additive assumption breaks down.
30	
31	\subsection{Compounding Effect}
32	\label{sec:compounding}
33	
34	When many heads are simultaneously quantized to 2-bit, per-head distortions compound non-additively.
35	The mechanism is straightforward: each head's quantized output feeds into the residual stream, and truncation errors from multiple 2-bit heads accumulate through subsequent layers.
36	When the number of 2-bit heads is small, these errors are absorbed by the remaining high-precision heads.
37	As the count grows, cumulative errors exceed the capacity of the residual stream to compensate, and PPL degrades super-linearly.
38	
39	\begin{figure}[t]
40	\centering
41	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_compounding_curve.pdf}
42	\caption{PPL on Qwen2.5-7B ($4\times$ compression) as a function of $k$, the maximum number of 2-bit heads. Too few 2-bit heads waste budget on 4-bit; too many trigger compounding. The minimum occurs at $k{=}8$.}
43	\label{fig:compounding}
44	\end{figure}
45	
46	Unconstrained solvers are blind to this effect because the additive objective underestimates the cost of large-scale 2-bit assignment.
47	On Qwen2.5-7B, unconstrained greedy assigns 68 heads to 2-bit and achieves 32.45 PPL; unconstrained MCKP assigns 75 heads and achieves 36.92---both far worse than uniform 4-bit (15.45).
48	Standard-resolution profiling detects non-zero $d_h(2)$ for only 37 of 112 heads; the remaining 75 heads have $d_h(2) \approx 0$, so most 2-bit assignments appear free to the additive objective.
49	The resulting additive prediction is $\sum_h d_h(b_h) + \text{baseline} \approx 11$ PPL---$3\text{--}4\times$ lower than the actual 32--37 PPL, because the compounding interaction between simultaneously quantized heads is invisible to per-head profiling.
50	
51	This compounding is specific to 2-bit quantization.
52	At 4-bit and above, per-head distortions are small enough that additivity holds even when all heads share the same bit-width (uniform 4-bit achieves 15.45 PPL, close to the sum-of-distortions prediction).
53	The qualitative difference arises because 2-bit quantization has far larger per-head distortion, saturating the error tolerance of the residual stream.
54	
55	Figure~\ref{fig:compounding} shows the relationship between $k$ (the maximum number of 2-bit heads) and PPL on Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression.
56	The curve is U-shaped: at $k{=}0$ (uniform 4-bit), PPL is 15.45; allowing a few 2-bit heads reduces PPL by freeing budget for 8-bit heads on sensitive positions, reaching a minimum of 11.23 at $k{=}8$; beyond this point, compounding drives PPL upward, reaching 35.35 at $k{=}75$.
57	
58	\subsection{Cardinality Constraint}
59	\label{sec:cardinality}
60	
61	The compounding effect motivates a simple addition to Eq.~\eqref{eq:objective}: a cardinality constraint on 2-bit assignments.
62	\begin{equation}
63	\label{eq:constraint}
64	\sum_{h=1}^{H} \mathbb{1}[b_h = 2] \leq k.
65	\end{equation}
66	
67	The constraint parameter $k$ is selected by a small-scale sweep on calibration data: solve the constrained problem for each candidate $k$, evaluate calibration PPL, and pick the value at the minimum of the U-shaped curve (Figure~\ref{fig:compounding}).
68	For Qwen2.5-7B with 112 KV heads, $k{=}8$ ($\sim$7\% of heads).
69	
70	The constraint is a single linear inequality, compatible with any solver---greedy, MCKP, or integer linear programming---and adds negligible overhead to the optimization.
71	
72	A natural question is whether Layer-0 heads require explicit protection, since attention heads in the first layer are known to carry disproportionate importance.
73	On Qwen2.5-7B, the profiler assigns very high distortion to Layer-0 heads at 2-bit: L0H0 increases PPL by 31.9\% relative to the bf16 baseline (9.81 $\to$ 12.94), L0H2 by 23.2\% (9.81 $\to$ 12.09), L0H3 by 11.7\% (9.81 $\to$ 10.96).
74	These values are large enough that no solver would assign 2-bit to Layer-0 under any reasonable budget.
75	We verify this empirically: running the solver with and without manual Layer-0 exclusion produces identical allocations across all 112 heads.
76	No manual exclusion rule is needed; the profiler signal is sufficient.
77	
78	\subsection{Solver Equivalence}
79	\label{sec:solver_equiv}
80	
81	\begin{table}[t]
82	\centering
83	\small
84	\caption{Solver comparison on Qwen2.5-7B at $4\times$ compression. Unconstrained solvers over-allocate 2-bit heads and fail catastrophically. The cardinality constraint ($k{\leq}8$) makes greedy and MCKP produce identical allocations.\protect\footnotemark}
85	\label{tab:solver_equiv}
86	\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
87	\toprule
88	Solver & Constraint & PPL & \multicolumn{3}{c}{Bit distribution} \\
89	 & & & 2-bit & 4-bit & 8/16-bit \\
90	\midrule
91	Greedy & None & 32.45 & 68 & 30 & 14 \\
92	MCKP & None & 36.92 & 75 & 33 & 4 \\
93	Greedy & $k{\leq}8$ & 11.23 & 8 & 100 & 4 \\
94	MCKP & $k{\leq}8$ & 11.23 & 8 & 100 & 4 \\
95	Uniform & --- & 15.45 & 0 & 112 & 0 \\
96	\bottomrule
97	\end{tabular}
98	\end{table}
99	\footnotetext{Standard-resolution profiling; hires profiling (64 seq $\times$ 2048 tok) achieves 10.91 (Appendix~\ref{sec:profiling_resolution}).}
100	
101	With the cardinality constraint in place, greedy and MCKP produce identical results---not approximately, but exactly.
102	Table~\ref{tab:solver_equiv} shows that constrained greedy and constrained MCKP achieve the same PPL (11.23) with the same bit distribution on Qwen2.5-7B.
103	We verify this at the per-head level across three models:
104	
105	\begin{itemize}[nosep]
106	\item \textbf{Qwen2.5-7B:} 112/112 heads receive identical bit-widths.
107	\item \textbf{Llama-3.1-8B:} 256/256 heads identical.
108	\item \textbf{Mistral-7B-v0.3:} 255/256 heads identical. The single difference is a zero-distortion tie between two heads at 4-bit and 8-bit, with no PPL impact.
109	\end{itemize}
110	
111	The constraint narrows the feasible set enough that greedy's locally optimal decisions are globally optimal.
112	Without it, greedy cascades into excessive 2-bit allocation: each additional 2-bit head looks locally beneficial (freeing budget) but contributes to the compounding effect that degrades global PPL.
113	The cardinality constraint breaks this cascade by capping the number of 2-bit heads, aligning local and global optima.
114	
115	The practical implication is that practitioners can use the simpler $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm instead of MCKP without sacrificing optimality.
116	
117	To verify that constrained MCKP is near-optimal, we perform a per-layer brute-force oracle on Qwen2.5-7B: for each of the 28 layers, we enumerate all $4^4{=}256$ bit-width assignments to the 4 KV heads and select the allocation minimizing per-layer PPL.
118	Of the 8 layers with non-trivial (non-all-4-bit) allocations, MCKP matches the oracle on 5; the remaining 3 have a maximum gap of 0.018 PPL---0.4\% of the constrained-vs-uniform improvement (4.53 PPL)---due to within-layer 2-bit head position swaps with no change to the per-layer bit budget.
119	Combined with the greedy--MCKP equivalence above, this closes the optimality chain: a simple $O(H \log H)$ greedy algorithm (runtime 0.005s) produces allocations within 0.02 PPL of the brute-force optimum.
